headline: High-risk default filesystem and network overlap; prompt-injection and cascading-error pathways are plausible, while compliance risk is lower and mostly indirect.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and parse tool outputs; Rasa exposes chat channels and allowlisted egress. If CrewAI writes attacker-controlled content into shared files or messages that Rasa later treats as dialogue, injection is plausible. The pair lacks a documented shared channel, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents exchange content through a shared file, queue, or chat channel without provenance tags
IF Rasa consumes CrewAI-generated text as dialogue or policy text
mitigations: Separate their workspaces
Add provenance labels to all inter-agent messages
Disable file-based handoff between agents
Require human review before Rasa acts on CrewAI text

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI touches developer-passed crew data and has broad network egress; Rasa handles text and voice and can send messages through external channels. A shared workspace or copied transcript could leak sensitive crew data into outbound bot traffic. Because no direct shared filesystem is documented, this is inferred but still plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF CrewAI receives sensitive crew inputs and writes them to files or stdout
IF Rasa forwards those transcripts to Messenger, Slack, Telegram, or Twilio
mitigations: Keep sensitive inputs out of shared files
Redact transcripts before passing them to Rasa
Restrict Rasa channels to test tenants
Turn off CrewAI network egress for sensitive runs
Use separate credentials per agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: CrewAI can write the host filesystem and spawn subprocesses; Rasa is a multi-instance-unsupported chatbot framework with external channel integrations. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or deployment artifacts, they can overwrite each other’s state. No locking or isolation is documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or config files
IF the orchestrator does not provide file locks or per-agent isolation
mitigations: Give each agent a separate directory
Mount shared artifacts read-only
Serialize writes with a lock file
Run Rasa and CrewAI in separate containers

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI can generate intermediate outputs from crew data, and Rasa can route text through conversational channels. If Rasa treats CrewAI output as authoritative without verification, a mistaken plan or fact can cascade into user-facing bot responses. The interaction is inferred rather than directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF CrewAI output is fed into Rasa responses or dialogue policies
IF no validation step checks CrewAI facts before Rasa sends them
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require citations or schema checks on CrewAI output
Have Rasa fall back to canned responses on parse failure
Log and sample-review inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, while Rasa handles text and voice with channel integrations. The profiles do not show a residency, certification, or retention mismatch, so only a generic compliance gap is visible. I do not cite only one agent because the risk depends on their combined data flow, but the evidence is thin.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed from CrewAI into Rasa channels without a DPA or retention policy
IF logs retain transcripts longer than policy allows
mitigations: Classify data before routing it
Set explicit retention limits on bot logs
Disable regulated-data channels
Review vendor DPAs and residency settings
